tourniquet application: Apply 5-7cm ABOVE wound (never over joint). COMMERCIAL: pull tight, rotate windlass rod until bleeding stops, lock, write time on skin with marker. IMPROVISED: minimum 5cm wide material (NOT rope or wire), place pad underneath, reef knot, insert stick, twist until bleeding stops, secure stick. MAX 2 hours before irreversible tissue damage. Write application time always. Never remove in field — only surgeons remove tourniquets. CPR continues despite tourniquet.
CPR adult: Call emergency services first (or have someone call) and get an AED if one is near. COMPRESSION ONLY if untrained: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, 100-120 per minute, 5-6cm deep, let the chest come all the way back up. TRAINED: 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths. Rhythm: the song Stayin' Alive is about 100 per minute. Keep going until an AED is ready, trained help takes over, or the person starts breathing. CHILD (1 year to puberty): one or two hands, about 5cm deep (a third of the chest), 30:2. INFANT (under 1 year): two fingers just below the nipple line, about 4cm deep, 30:2 for one rescuer (15:2 with two trained rescuers). AED: turn it on, follow the voice prompts, restart compressions right after a shock.
choking adult Heimlich: CONSCIOUS ADULT: 5 back blows with heel of hand between shoulder blades, alternating with 5 abdominal thrusts (just above navel, upward and inward). Continue until object expelled or unconscious. UNCONSCIOUS: lay flat, look in mouth before each breath attempt, never blind finger sweep. PREGNANT or OBESE: chest thrusts instead of abdominal. INFANT: 5 back blows face-down, 5 chest thrusts face-up, never abdominal thrusts. Self-treatment: thrust abdomen over chair back or hands over own fist.
severe bleeding control: PRIORITY ORDER: 1) Direct pressure — push HARD with cloth, maintain for 10 minutes without peeking. 2) Pack wound: push cloth or gauze deep into cavity with finger, maintain pressure. 3) Tourniquet for limb bleeding that does not stop with pressure. Wound packing with pressure is more effective than tourniquet for neck/groin/armpit injuries where tourniquet cannot be applied. Shock prevention: lay flat, elevate legs 30cm, keep warm, do not give fluids if unconscious.
burns treatment: COOL: run cool (not cold/ice) water over burn for minimum 20 minutes — stops ongoing tissue damage. Remove jewelry and non-stuck clothing. SEVERITY: first degree (redness only, no blisters) — cool, moisturize, no further treatment. Second degree (blisters present) — do NOT burst blisters, cover loosely, seek medical care. Third degree (white/charred, no pain in area) — do NOT cool large third degree (hypothermia risk), cover with sterile dressing, immediate evacuation. Chemical burns: continuous water flush 60 minutes minimum.
fracture management field: ASSUME FRACTURE if: significant mechanism, point tenderness, deformity, inability to bear weight. SPLINT IN POSITION FOUND — do not attempt to realign except if no distal pulse (circulation compromise). Splint extends one joint above and below fracture. IMPROVISED: straight sticks padded with clothing, tied snugly but not tight (check circulation every 30 min). FEMUR (thigh bone): traction splint needed — improvise with two straight poles and bandanas for traction ties — blood loss can be 2 liters internally. SPINE injury: immobilize entire spine, do not bend neck, log-roll for movement.
anaphylaxis severe allergic reaction: SIGNS: hives + breathing difficulty + low blood pressure — can kill in minutes. EPINEPHRINE (EpiPen): inject outer thigh through clothing, hold 10 seconds; repeat in 5-15 min if no improvement. POSITION: sitting upright if breathing difficulty; lying down with legs raised if blood pressure low (never let them stand). AIRWAY: be prepared to perform CPR. ANTIHISTAMINES (Benadryl): slow-acting, NOT substitute for epinephrine, gives secondary support. EVACUATION: mandatory even after epinephrine — anaphylaxis can return 4-8h later (biphasic reaction).
hypothermia treatment: MILD (32-35C, shivering): remove wet clothing, add dry insulation, warm sweet liquid if alert, shelter from wind. MODERATE (28-32C, confusion, no shivering): horizontal position, handle gently (cardiac arrest risk from movement), heat packs to armpits/groin/neck only, NO direct heat to extremities. SEVERE below 28C: unconscious, rigid — NEVER assume dead; continue CPR; a patient is not dead until warm and dead. REWARMING: core first, never periphery first (can cause rewarming shock). Evacuation is definitive treatment.
heat stroke: HEAT STROKE = life-threatening (core temp above 40C with altered mental status). DISTINGUISH from heat exhaustion: heat stroke = hot DRY skin + confusion; heat exhaustion = cool/clammy + weakness + normal mental status. TREATMENT: immediate aggressive cooling — immerse in cold water or cover with ice/cold wet cloths, fan continuously. Target: reduce core temp to 39C in 30 minutes. Do NOT give fluids to unconscious patient. Aspirin/Tylenol ineffective for heat stroke (not fever-mediated). Evacuate after cooling.
snakebite management: WHAT TO DO: move away, keep victim calm and still (slows venom spread), immobilize bitten limb at or below heart level, remove jewelry, mark swelling edge with pen + time. EVACUATE IMMEDIATELY — antivenom is the treatment. WHAT NOT TO DO: do NOT cut and suck, do NOT apply tourniquet, do NOT apply ice, do NOT use electricity. Identify snake by photo if possible without risk. Most snakebites in field: triangular head + heat pits = pit viper; hood display = cobra. 80% of bites from venomous snakes do not inject significant venom.
wound cleaning infection prevention: IRRIGATION: most important step — 200-500mL saline or clean water at pressure (syringe with 18g needle or bag with pinhole creates ideal pressure). Copious irrigation reduces infection rate by 80%. DEBRIDEMENT: remove all visible debris and necrotic tissue. CLOSURE: close clean wounds within 6h (primary closure); contaminated or animal bite wounds left open (secondary closure). SIGNS OF INFECTION (24-72h): redness spreading from wound edge, warmth, increasing pain, pus, red streaks (lymphangitis = serious), fever.
shock recognition treatment: TYPES: hemorrhagic (blood loss), distributive (septic, anaphylactic), cardiogenic (heart failure). UNIVERSAL SIGNS: weak/rapid pulse, cold/clammy skin, altered mental status, rapid breathing. TREATMENT: lay flat + legs elevated 30cm (except chest injury or difficulty breathing — sitting upright). Stop bleeding source. Keep warm. IV fluids if available. Supplemental oxygen if available. Do NOT give oral fluids to shock patient — aspiration risk. Rapid evacuation is definitive treatment for all shock types.
wound closure steri-strips butterfly: STERI-STRIPS/BUTTERFLY CLOSURE: dry wound completely, apply tincture of benzoin to skin (not wound) to improve adhesion. Place strips perpendicular to wound, pull edges together gently, apply strips 3mm apart. IMPROVISED BUTTERFLY: cut adhesive tape in a dumbbell shape. For deeper wounds requiring sutures: cover with sterile dressing, evacuate within 24h for surgical closure. Scalp wounds: staples preferred; hair ties useful as improvised wound closure (tie strands together across wound).
appendicitis recognition: CLASSIC SIGNS: pain starting around navel migrating to right lower quadrant (McBurney's point), nausea/vomiting, fever (low-grade initially). REBOUND TENDERNESS: press slowly on right lower quadrant, release quickly — pain on release confirms peritoneal irritation. PSOAS TEST: patient on left side, extend right leg backward — pain = inflamed appendix. ROVSING SIGN: press left lower quadrant — referred pain in right lower quadrant. CHILDREN: often atypical presentation. EVACUATION: mandatory — perforated appendix causes peritonitis and sepsis within 24-48h.
concussion assessment: SIGNS: headache, confusion, memory loss for event, brief loss of consciousness, nausea, sensitivity to light/noise, balance problems. GRADING no longer used — any concussion requires complete cognitive rest. REST PROTOCOL: 24-48h no screens, no exertion, sleep encouraged. RETURN TO ACTIVITY: only when completely symptom-free at rest. RED FLAGS requiring emergency evacuation: loss of consciousness over 1 minute, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, unequal pupils, seizure, weakness/numbness in extremities, increasing confusion.
sepsis recognition: SEPSIS = life-threatening organ dysfunction from infection. CRITERIA (Sepsis-3): suspected infection PLUS quick SOFA — 1) respiratory rate over 22/min; 2) altered mental status; 3) systolic BP under 100mmHg. Any 2 of 3 = presumptive sepsis, begin evacuation. FIELD SIGNS: high fever or very low temperature, rapid heart rate over 100, rapid breathing, confusion or lethargy, decreased urine output. SOURCE: most commonly lung, urinary tract, wound, abdomen. TREATMENT: IV antibiotics + IV fluids within 1 hour of recognition = dramatically improves survival.
dehydration assessment treatment: MILD (3-5% body weight): thirst, slightly decreased urine output, normal mental status. Oral rehydration solution (ORS): 1L water + 6 tsp sugar + 1/2 tsp salt (WHO formula). MODERATE (6-9%): dry mouth, headache, dark urine, nausea, weakness. Aggressive ORS or IV if available. SEVERE (10%+): confusion, no urine, rapid weak pulse, sunken eyes, unable to stand — medical emergency. VOMITING: small frequent sips every 5 min, anti-emetic if available, IV fluids if not retaining oral. CHILDREN: dehydrate faster, oral rehydration is life-saving intervention.
dental emergency field: TOOTHACHE: clove oil or eugenol on cotton ball applied directly to tooth for temporary pain relief. LOST FILLING: temporary filling material (zinc oxide paste), softened candle wax, or sugarless gum as temporary seal. DENTAL ABSCESS: ibuprofen for pain, amoxicillin 500mg every 8h if available, evacuate — abscess can spread to jaw/neck/brain. KNOCKED-OUT TOOTH: rinse without scrubbing root, replace in socket immediately or store in milk/saliva, evacuate within 1h for reimplantation chance. BROKEN JAW: soft diet, support with bandage under chin, evacuate.
eye injury field: FOREIGN BODY: irrigate with clean water or saline, do not rub, flip upper eyelid if object not found. Metal fragments require magnetic extraction at facility — do not probe. CHEMICAL SPLASH: immediate continuous irrigation for minimum 20 minutes, hold eye open, pivot entire face under water stream. PENETRATING INJURY: do NOT remove object, cover with rigid eye shield (cup), patch uninjured eye to reduce sympathetic movement, immediate evacuation. SNOWBLINDNESS: cool wet cloth on closed eyes, rest in darkness, ibuprofen for pain — resolves in 12-24h if eyes rest.
improvised stretcher: TWO-POLE STRETCHER: thread two jackets (zipped, sleeves turned inside) onto two poles 2m long; poles through sleeves, jacket forms carry surface. TEST: load weight before use, poles must extend 30cm beyond carriers. BLANKET STRETCHER: 3 people each grip edge, patient in center — no poles needed short distance. PATIENT PACKAGING: if suspected spinal injury, log roll onto stretcher maintaining head-neck-spine alignment, pad all voids. CARRY: 4-person minimum for spinal injury; 2-person for limb injury. Downhill carry: feet first; uphill: head first.
altitude sickness recognition: ACUTE MOUNTAIN SICKNESS (AMS): headache plus nausea/vomiting OR fatigue OR dizziness OR poor sleep at altitude. MILD: treat with rest, hydration, ibuprofen, do not ascend higher until symptoms resolve completely. HIGH ALTITUDE PULMONARY EDEMA (HAPE): breathlessness at rest, productive cough (pink frothy), rapid deterioration — IMMEDIATE DESCENT is primary treatment, every 300m helps. HIGH ALTITUDE CEREBRAL EDEMA (HACE): confusion, ataxia (stumbling walk test), severe headache — IMMEDIATE DESCENT, dexamethasone if available, portable hyperbaric bag if available. GOLDEN RULE: never ascend with AMS symptoms.
improvised medications: PAIN/FEVER: willow bark tea (salicin), meadowsweet (also salicin). ANTIBACTERIAL WOUND WASH: diluted honey (high osmolarity kills bacteria), garlic extract, diluted pine pitch. ANTI-INFLAMMATORY: turmeric (curcumin), ginger root. DIARRHEA: blackberry root/bark tea (tannins), activated charcoal if available. CONSTIPATION: senna leaves tea (use cautiously). COUGH SUPPRESSANT: thyme tea, honey. ANTISEPTIC: diluted alcohol, diluted iodine from first aid kit, diluted hydrogen peroxide for wound wash only. NOTE: all improvised medications are temporizing — evacuate when possible.
drowning response: WATER SAFETY: do not enter water to save panicking drowning victim without flotation device — they will push you under. Throw flotation device, reach with stick/rope, row to them. AFTER RESCUE: if unresponsive and not breathing, begin CPR immediately — even after extended submersion in cold water, neurological recovery is possible. Secondary drowning: monitor all submersion victims for 24h for delayed respiratory symptoms. Hypothermia is likely concurrent — manage both. Do NOT hold upside down to drain water — this delays CPR.
diabetic emergency field: HYPOGLYCEMIA (low blood sugar) — common emergency: shakiness, sweating, confusion, unconsciousness. CONSCIOUS: give fast sugar — 4 glucose tablets, 120mL juice, 3 hard candies. Repeat in 15 min if no improvement. UNCONSCIOUS: do NOT give oral fluids (aspiration); glucagon injection if available; rub glucose gel on inner cheek. HYPERGLYCEMIA (high blood sugar): gradual onset, fruity breath, large urine output, confusion — needs insulin and IV fluids, medical emergency. In field without supplies: treat any unconscious diabetic as hypoglycemia first (safer error).
